clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant inheritance; look for a multigenerational family history of early gout and progressive chronic kidney disease.
Hyperuricaemia and clinical gout typically appear in adolescence or early adulthood, often out of proportion to the degree of renal impairment.
A characteristically low fractional excretion of urate reflects enhanced proximal tubular urate reabsorption and helps distinguish it from urate overproduction.
Urinary sediment is bland with little or no proteinuria, and the kidneys are normal-sized or small, sometimes with small medullary cysts.
It is the prototypic autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease due to UMOD (uromodulin) mutations, formerly grouped with medullary cystic kidney disease type 2.
Diagnosis rests on UMOD genetic testing; renal biopsy shows tubulointerstitial fibrosis with intracellular uromodulin aggregates in the thick ascending limb.
Urate-lowering therapy controls gout but has not been shown reliably to slow progression of the kidney disease.
Consider the sibling ADTKD subtypes (REN, HNF1B, MUC1) when hyperuricaemia is absent or additional features are present.
reference.pathophysiology: Familial juvenile hyperuricaemic nephropathy is most often caused by heterozygous mutations in UMOD, the gene encoding uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall protein), the most abundant protein secreted by epithelial cells of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Most pathogenic variants are missense changes that disturb conserved cysteine residues, causing the mutant protein to misfold and become retained within the endoplasmic reticulum. The resulting endoplasmic reticulum stress and impaired trafficking injure tubular cells and drive progressive tubulointerstitial fibrosis. Reduced delivery of functional uromodulin to the apical membrane also perturbs sodium chloride handling through the NKCC2 cotransporter and the ROMK channel, promoting subtle volume contraction, secondary activation of the renin-angiotensin system and compensatory upregulation of proximal tubular urate reabsorption, which produces the hallmark hyperuricaemia and gout. The condition forms part of the autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease spectrum, and its severity and age at end-stage kidney disease vary even within a single family.
additionalDifferentials: ADTKD-REN (renin mutations) with childhood anaemia, hyperkalaemia and a tendency to hypotension.
ADTKD-HNF1B with renal cysts, early-onset diabetes, hypomagnesaemia and genital tract anomalies.
ADTKD-MUC1 (mucin-1) causing tubulointerstitial disease without prominent hyperuricaemia.
Nephronophthisis and other medullary cystic kidney diseases.
Primary (lifestyle-related) gout coexisting with independent chronic kidney disease.
Lead nephropathy and other chronic tubulointerstitial nephritides that raise urate.
Glycogen storage disease and other metabolic causes of early hyperuricaemia.
additionalInvestigations: Serum urate with calculation of the fractional excretion of urate.
Serial renal function and estimated glomerular filtration rate.
Urinalysis and quantification of proteinuria, which is typically minimal.
Renal ultrasound to assess kidney size and detect medullary cysts.
Targeted UMOD sequencing, extended to an ADTKD gene panel (REN, HNF1B, MUC1) if negative.
Screening of first-degree relatives with serum urate and renal function.
Renal biopsy with uromodulin immunostaining when genetic testing is inconclusive.
redFlags: Accelerating decline in renal function or progression towards end-stage kidney disease.
Refractory or tophaceous gout despite urate-lowering therapy.
Hyperkalaemia, anaemia or hypotension in childhood, suggesting an ADTKD-REN subtype.
New nephrotic-range proteinuria, which should prompt a search for an alternative diagnosis.
reference.prognosis: Progression to end-stage kidney disease is usual, generally during adulthood, although the age at which this occurs varies considerably within and between families. Kidney transplantation is successful, as the disease does not recur in the allograft.
pitfalls: Attributing early gout to diet or alcohol and overlooking an inherited tubulointerstitial disease.
Expecting significant proteinuria or an active sediment, whose absence can be falsely reassuring.
Assuming that controlling urate will prevent progression of the kidney disease.
Failing to take a detailed multigenerational family history of gout and renal failure.
Overlooking sibling ADTKD subtypes when hyperuricaemia is mild or absent.
references: KDIGO consensus report on autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease
management: Start early urate-lowering therapy with a xanthine oxidase inhibitor (allopurinol or febuxostat) to control hyperuricaemia and prevent recurrent gout
Treat acute gout flares with anti-inflammatory therapy (colchicine, an NSAID or a corticosteroid) chosen according to renal function
Institute nephroprotective management of the progressive tubulointerstitial disease with blood-pressure control and avoidance of nephrotoxins
Monitor renal function serially and prepare for renal replacement therapy as disease advances
Offer kidney transplantation for end-stage disease, noting the condition does not recur in the allograft
Perform UMOD genetic testing, extending to an ADTKD gene panel if negative, with counselling and screening of first-degree relatives by serum urate and renal function
Provide multidisciplinary nephrology and clinical genetics follow-up
